description_full: Starbucks Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, operates as a roaster, marketer, and retailer of coffee internationally. The company operates through three segments: North America, International, and Channel Development. Its stores offer coffee, tea, and other beverages, roasted whole beans and ground coffees, complementary food, packaged coffees, single-serve products, and ready-to-drink beverages; and various food products, such as pastries, breakfast sandwiches, and lunch items. The company also licenses its trademarks through licensed stores, and grocery and foodservice accounts. The company offers its products under the Starbucks Coffee, Teavana, Ethos, and Starbucks Reserve brands. Starbucks Corporation was founded in 1971 and is based in Seattle, Washington.

financial_summary: Starbucks Corporation is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $121.4B market cap on $37.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +2% over the past three years and +6% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 53% against a 9% cost of capital — a 44-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $3.7B in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.97× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is moderate at 2.5× net debt/EBITDA, serviceable in normal conditions but worth watching through a downturn, and interest coverage runs at 6.9×.

Shareholder yield of 2.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 40% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Payout ratio looks stretched — the dividend’s own margin of safety is thin
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Insiders are overwhelmingly selling (100% sell ratio) — the people who know the business want less of it
Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sect: Its 10% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Cyclical median (7%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.23x).
It accounts for 0.7% of sector revenue and 0.9% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-2.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 9% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 5% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 28% and a beta of 0.98, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.48 vs 5y 0.97), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $688.4M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 40% in the 2020 crash, 40% in the 2022 bear market and 65% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $75.88 (margin of safety -40%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 10%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $53.98 to $106 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 48.2 vs 18.8, EV/EBITDA 24.6 vs 10.7 and P/FCF 32.6 vs 16.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 68% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.1% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 30 covering analysts target $111 on average, 4% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 53% clears the cost of capital of 8.9% by 44pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.75).
It converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.97x.
It spends 1.0% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is moderate at 2.5x net debt to EBITDA ($3.9B of cash against $13.3B of debt), above the 1.5x gate, with interest covered 6.9x.
The current ratio of 0.76 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.8% over 3 years, 5.5% over 5 years and 5.9% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 2% of profits supports about 1.2% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -3.8% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs only 0.8x depreciation (3.3% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 14, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 87%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (9 sales, net $1.6M sold).
It returns 2.3% a year to shareholders (2.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.7% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It pays out 112% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: CEO pay is $11.1M, and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
